body.heading: Pokémon on Vinted: great prices, real fakes
paragraphs: Pokémon cards are one of the highest-volume collectible categories on Vinted, and the prices can be genuinely good — below what you'd pay on a specialist marketplace or a card shop. Sealed products, singles and bulk lots all move constantly, because it's an evergreen hobby with a steady stream of new and returning buyers.

The catch is that Pokémon cards are counterfeited at industrial scale, and on a marketplace like Vinted — where sellers aren't card specialists — fakes slip through constantly. The difference between a bargain and a rip-off comes down to a few checks you can do from photos.
This guide covers how to spot a fake, how to judge condition (which drives the price), and how to catch the genuine listings before they're gone.

body.heading: How to spot fake Pokémon cards
paragraphs: 1. **Compare the back.** The most reliable check is the back of the card — a genuine Pokémon card has a distinctive deep-blue back with a specific border and swirl pattern. Fakes are almost always a slightly wrong shade of blue, or the border is off. If you can, compare against a card you know is real.

2. **Check the texture.** Full-art cards (V, VMAX, EX, GX and most modern rares) are textured — they have a fine raised pattern you can feel. A full-art card with no texture is a dead giveaway. The main exception is Trainer Gallery cards, which are full-art but untextured.

3. **Look at the font.** The Pokémon card font is distinctive and hard to mimic. Fakes often have slightly wrong lettering, spacing or weight. Compare the card against a reference image of the same card.

4. **Check the holo foiling.** Genuine holo patterns run in a specific direction and don't cover the whole card uniformly. If the holo is overly shiny, covers everything, or runs vertically top-to-bottom without variation, it's likely fake.
5. **The light test.** Genuine cards let a little light through but stay largely opaque; fakes are often either see-through or completely solid. It's a rough check, but useful as a first filter.
6. **The price.** A rare card or sealed product at a fraction of market value is almost always fake. If it's too good to be true, it is.
For the general fake-spotting framework, see [how to spot fakes on Vinted](/guides/vinted-scams-buyer-protection).

body.heading: Judging condition (this is what drives the price)
paragraphs: Condition is everything with Pokémon cards, and it's the thing sellers on Vinted are least reliable about. The same card can be worth a few pounds damaged or hundreds in mint condition, so you need to judge it from the photos, not the seller's description.

Ask for clear photos of the front and back, and check for: edge wear, corner damage (bent or whitened corners), surface scratches on the holo, and centring (how evenly the card is framed by its border). A card that's off-centre is worth less, and one with edge wear or whitened corners has dropped out of "near mint".

For sealed products, check the packaging is intact and untampered — resealed packs and boxes are a common scam on every marketplace, not just Vinted. See [what actually sells on Vinted](/guides/what-sells-on-vinted) for how collectibles fit the broader picture.

body.heading: What to buy (and what to skip)
paragraphs: Buy singles you can verify with clear photos, and sealed products only from sellers with a good track record and clear packaging shots. Modern full-art rares and vintage holos hold value best and are the most worth an alert.

Skip bulk lots unless they're genuinely cheap and you're happy with a mixed-condition gamble — bulk lots are where fakes and heavily-played cards hide. And be wary of sellers listing dozens of "rare" cards at low prices, which is a classic counterfeit pattern.
For the resale angle, read [how to sell on Vinted](/guides/how-to-sell-on-vinted) — Pokémon is a reliable category to source, but authenticating and grading every card is the price of entry.

body.heading: Why an alert beats refreshing the search
paragraphs: Genuine cards and sealed products at good prices sell within minutes of being listed — the fakes and the overpriced listings are the ones that linger. If you're checking manually, you're always behind the people who get notified instantly.

A saved-search alert watches for your exact criteria — set, card, price cap — and pings you the moment something matching is listed. You still run the back-comparison and texture checks before buying, but you're no longer the last person to see the listing.
[Set up an alert for the cards you want](/guides/vinted-price-alert) and you'll catch the genuine deals before they're gone.

faq.question: Are Pokémon cards on Vinted real?
faq.answer: Many are genuine, but Pokémon cards are heavily counterfeited, so check before you buy. Compare the card back against a known-genuine card, check full-art cards are textured, look for font differences, and be suspicious of rare cards priced far below market value.

faq.question: How can I spot a fake Pokémon card?
faq.answer: Compare the back of the card against a real one — fakes are usually a slightly wrong shade of blue or off border. Then check full-art cards are textured, look at the font, and check the holo pattern runs in the right direction. Rare cards at a fraction of market value are almost always fake.

faq.question: What should I check before buying Pokémon cards on Vinted?
faq.answer: Ask for clear front and back photos, then judge condition — edge wear, whitened corners, surface scratches and centring all drive the value. For sealed products, check the packaging is intact and untampered, as resealed packs are a common scam.

faq.question: Do Pokémon cards hold their value on Vinted?
faq.answer: Yes — modern full-art rares and vintage holos hold value well, and it's one of Vinted's highest-volume collectible categories. Condition is everything, so a mint card is worth far more than the same card with edge wear.

faq.question: Should I buy Pokémon card bulk lots on Vinted?
faq.answer: Only if they're genuinely cheap and you're happy with a mixed-condition gamble — bulk lots are where fakes and heavily-played cards hide. For anything valuable, buy singles you can verify with clear photos, or sealed products from a seller with a good track record.
